                            STATE OF ALASKA’S
                           MOTION TO INTERVENE

      Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s Rules

of Practice and Procedure, the State of Alaska (“Alaska”) requests for leave to

intervene in Docket No. P-15423-000. 18 C.F.R. § 385.214.

I.    COMMUNICATIONS

The State requests that the following individual be listed on the official

service list and any communications regarding this filing should be addressed to

the following:

 II. INTERESTS OF THE STATE INTERVENOR

      Alaska has constitutionally mandated interests in encouraging the

responsible development of natural resources within the State. Alaska Const., Art.

VIII, §§ 1, 2 (The Alaska Constitution requires Alaska to manage resources for the

maximum benefit and use by its people.). As a sovereign, Alaska has a universal

interest in the health, welfare, and safety of its residents across the State. Alaska

Const. Art. VII, §§ 4, 5. Wildlife is reserved to the people for common use, and

must be “utilized, developed, and maintained on the sustained yield principle,

subject to preferences among beneficial uses.” Alaska Const. Art. VIII, §§ 3, 4. As

to water rights, the Alaska Const. Art. VIII § 13 provides:

      All surface and subsurface waters reserved to the people for
      common use, except mineral and medicinal waters, are subject
      to appropriation. Priority of appropriation shall give prior right.
      Except for public water supply, an appropriation of water shall
      be limited to stated purposes and subject to preferences among
      beneficial uses, concurrent or otherwise, as prescribed by law,
      and to the general reservation of fish and wildlife.

      The Alaska Constitution, Art. VIII, § 6, further establishes that “[l]ands and

interests in them, including submerged and tidal lands … constitute the state public

domain” and selection and use of such lands is governed by the State Legislature’s

delegation to the Alaska Department of Natural Resources, which includes leasing

of “any part of the public domain or interests therein.” Id. at §7. Importantly, any

sale or grant of state land requires “reservation to the State of all resources as may

 be required by Congress or the State.” Id. at § 9. And the Alaska Constitution

further prohibits any “disposal or lease of state lands, or interests therein” absent

“prior public notice or other safeguards of the public interest as may be prescribed

by law.” Id. at § 10. Likewise, the Alaska Constitution protects access to navigable

waters. Id. at § 6.

       Alaska’s role in management of natural resource development, commerce,

utilities, marine transportation and fisheries within the proposed project’s vicinity

is vast. To this end, Congress has granted Alaska with concurrent civil and

criminal jurisdiction over federal lands and waters located within the boundaries of

our sovereign state. Pub. L. No. 85-508, §11(b) (1958, as amended) and exercises

extensive taxing, police and regulatory powers. See Alaska Stat.§§ 43.55; 43.56;

43.20; 31.05.027 (jurisdiction of the Alaska Oil and Gas Conservation

Commission); AS 42.05.101 (powers and duties of the Alaska Regulatory

Commission). Alaska also has responsibilities for connecting communities and

helping sustain healthy subsistence throughout Alaska. Alaska Stat. § 19.05.125.

       As a sovereign state, Alaska owns the mineral and surface estate associated

with state land and waters in Cook Inlet, and further acts as a regulator, taxing

authority, and advocates for the interests of its residents. Likewise, Alaska, as a

sovereign and landowner, has an interest in energy security for the State and

Nation and through the Alaska Department of Natural Resources and the Alaska

State of Alaska Motion to Intervene
FERC Docket No. P-15423-000                                                 Page 3 of 6
 Oil and Gas Conservation Commission, regulates oil and gas development within

throughout Cook Inlet. To a large extent, this includes the federal waters of Cook

Inlet, whereby Congress under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act (“OCSLA”)

recognized the interests of Alaska through the mandatory consultation provisions,

co-management authorities, and revenue sharing from mineral leasing activity.

       Alaska frequently participates in legal matters involving proposed

development of federal waters within Cook Inlet, 1 and has extensive interest in the

protection of waters within Cook Inlet, including those related to the management

and regulation of Alaska’s Cook Inlet oil and gas leasing program. 2 Alaska’s

participation in this matter would aid the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission

(“FERC”) and the parties.

III.   THE STATE IS ENTITLED TO INTERVENE

       Alaska’s participation is supported by Rule 214(b)(2)(iii) and (ii) and the

proceedings may impact state agencies allowed for intervention as a matter of right

under Rule 214(a)(2). The proposed project could have impacts on Alaska’s

economic and socio-economic development and outcomes. Responsible

 development of natural resources within Alaska are vital to the State’s economy,

financial stability and energy security. Any further advancement of the project

would require coordination with various state agencies, including at least the

Alaska Department of Natural Resources, Alaska Department of Fish and Game,

and Alaska Department of Environmental Quality.


IV.   STATE OF ALASKA’S POSITION

      Pursuant to Rule 214(b)(1), any movant must state its position, if known,

and the basis in fact and law for that position. At this time, insufficient technical

information is available for Alaska to take a position on the proposed project. Any

proposed development of commercial-scale tidal energy and underwater data

center facility located in Cook Inlet waters would trigger the regulatory and police

powers of Alaska, particularly regarding utilization of State-owned waters and

tidelands, water quality, wildlife and fisheries, and intersection with existing

energy production from both State and Federal leases within the area. Likewise,

energy use and consumption are of critical importance to Alaska.

      Any proposed commercial-scale tidal energy and data facility located in

State or Federal waters of upper Cook Inlet, including associated state-owned

tidelands may involve land-use, environmental, fish and wildlife, water quality and

natural resource issues, and therefore the jurisdiction of Alaska. Intervention will

 ensure that Alaska receives sufficient notice and is informed of an opportunity to

actively participate on behalf of the state, its regulatory agencies, and citizens as

further information regarding this project becomes available.

IV.   CONCLUSION

      For the reasons set forth above, the State of Alaska requests to intervene in

Docket No. P-15423-000.
